content: The global burden of hepatitis C virus (HCV) co-infection among individuals living with HIV has been extensively studied through systematic reviews and meta-analyses, such as the one published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2016. Research has consistently highlighted the prevalence of HCV and HCV/HIV co-infection in various populations, including inpatients at the Kenyatta National Hospital in Kenya, as reported in the East African Medical Journal in 2005. Studies like the NICE SEROCO cohort in France have examined the prevalence of HCV antibodies in HIV-1-infected patients, as published in The Journal of Medical Virology in 1994. In the United States, cross-sectional analyses of adult AIDS Clinical Trials Group participants have revealed significant HCV prevalence among HIV-infected individuals, as detailed in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2002. Similarly, research conducted at Lyon University Hospitals in France between 1992 and 2002 explored the prevalence and sexual transmission risks of HCV in patients who acquired HIV through sexual intercourse, as published in The Journal of Viral Hepatitis in 2005. The evolving epidemiology and treatment paradigms of HIV and HCV co-infection have been reviewed in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2012, emphasizing the need for updated management strategies. Mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B virus (HBV) in sub-Saharan Africa has also been a focus of research, as highlighted in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2016. The natural history of chronic HBV infection, including its progression and outcomes, was reviewed in Seminars in Liver Disease in 2004. Perinatal transmission of HCV from HIV-1-infected mothers has been studied in the Women and Infants Transmission Study, with findings published in The Journal of Infectious Diseases in 1998. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses, such as those published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2014, have provided insights into the vertical transmission of HCV and its associated risk factors. The natural history of HCV infection acquired in infancy has been explored in studies like the one published in The Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2005. The role of horizontal transmission of HCV within households of infected children was investigated in a study published in The Journal of Pediatrics in 1993. Research has also examined HCV transmission dynamics in industrialized and resource-constrained settings, as reviewed in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2014. The sexual transmission of HCV among monogamous heterosexual couples was evaluated in the HCV Partners Study, with results published in Hepatology in 2013. The spread of HBV among household contacts in North India was studied in Intervirology in 2008, while the lack of evidence for sexual transmission of HCV among monogamous couples was reported in a 10-year prospective study published in The American Journal of Gastroenterology in 2004. The contributions of HBV and HCV infections to cirrhosis and primary liver cancer worldwide were reviewed in The Journal of Hepatology in 2006. Mathematical models estimating the global burden of HBV and the impact of vaccination were presented in The International Journal of Epidemiology in 2005. The management of mother-to-child transmission of HBV, including challenges and recommendations, was discussed in The Journal of Clinical Virology in 2016. Updated clinical practice guidelines for managing HBV in the Asia-Pacific region were published in Hepatology International in 2016. The epidemiology, disease burden, and prevention strategies for HBV were reviewed in The Journal of Viral Hepatitis in 2004. Evidence of declining HBV prevalence due to vaccination in central China was reported in The International Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2015. The prevalence of HBV infection in the United States during the vaccination era was analyzed in The Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2010. Comparative studies on the efficacy of antiviral treatments for chronic HBV, such as entecavir and tenofovir, were published in Hepatogastroenterology in 2015. Updates on HBV treatment strategies were reviewed in The Journal of Clinical and Translational Hepatology in 2014. The seroprevalence of HCV and HIV co-infection in sub-Saharan Africa was systematically reviewed in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2015. Global and regional mortality data from 235 causes of death, including liver-related conditions, were analyzed in The Lancet in 2012. The current and future burden of HCV infection under existing treatment paradigms was modeled in The Journal of Viral Hepatitis in 2014. The co-transmission of HCV and HIV among heterosexual couples was studied in Annals of Internal Medicine in 1991. Increasing mortality due to end-stage liver disease in HIV-infected patients was reported in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2001. The prevalence of HCV and associated high-risk practices in Egypt was explored in The Iranian Journal of Public Health in 2014. Cost-effectiveness analyses of HCV screening strategies in various populations, including birth cohorts and high-risk groups, have been extensively studied and published in journals such as Hepatology, The American Journal of Gastroenterology, and BMJ Open.
